disclosures: The cohort’s activity window is a fixed historical fortnight; yours is the last fourteen days. Comparable in length, not in calendar position — seasonality is not modelled.
The corpus is built from GH Archive, which sees PUBLIC repositories only. A private repository is still placed; the peer group it is placed against is public.

Your pull-request set is capped the way the corpus walk capped its own: the most recently updated pull requests, budgeted from the repository’s merge rate. Folding over your whole history instead would measure older threads than any cohort describes.

Thread ages are computed against the request clock, while the corpus froze them at observation. Both ask "was this thread at least 72 hours old when we looked", but your history is deeper, so your overdue and resolved rates read slightly worse for that reason alone.

report.narrative:
## What happened

Platform merged 54 pull requests this period. Half cleared in 71h from opening to merge, and the first human review landed after 28.8h on average. Review bots left 448 comments across the same work.

The biggest move was median time to first human review hours, up 26.2% against the previous period. The comparison covers all 5 repositories tracked across both periods.

## What to watch

- Time to first human review is the number to hold. It is the part of the wait that is entirely yours to spend, and it sits ahead of everything else in the queue.
- Bot comment volume keeps rising with pull-request volume. The question the Bots page answers is not how many, but how many were acted on.
- Coverage is stated above. Two repositories joined part-way through the reporting history, so the comparison runs on the stable subset and the headline figures do not.

body.headline: Across 10 merged pull requests a person actually worked on, time split 49% waiting for a reviewer, 39% waiting for the author, and 12% approved and waiting to merge. Half of pull requests merged within 2.5 days; three in four within 3 days. No single wait dominates here.

refusals.reason: No repository reached 12 merged pull requests with a human review so far this sprint.
No repository merged enough pull requests without a human review to name.

body.workHeadline: Counting working hours only, time split 37% waiting for a reviewer, 45% waiting for the author, and 18% approved and waiting to merge. Half of pull requests merged within 17 working hours of opening; three in four within 24 working hours.

budgets.sentence: Three in four pull requests had a first look within 7.2 working hours — over the 4-hour budget, inside the 8-hour limit.
Three in four pull requests that went back to their author had every reply within 14 working hours — over the 8-hour budget, inside the 16-hour limit.
Three in four approved pull requests merged within 4.1 working hours of approval — past the 4-hour limit.
Three in four pull requests merged within 24 working hours of opening — past the 16-hour limit.

body.markdown:
# Sync service runbook

How the Acme sync service pulls GitHub activity, writes it safely, and what to do when it misbehaves.

Source: sync-runbook.md · 5 sections

## Contents

- [How a sync runs](sections/01-how-a-sync-runs.md) — The phases of one repository sync, from the walk to the derived state.
- [Transactions](sections/02-transactions.md) — What must be written together, and what runs after the commit.
- [Schema changes](sections/03-schema-changes.md) — The rule for changing a table, and how migrations are registered.
- [Rate limits](sections/04-rate-limits.md) — How the sync spends the GitHub budget and what it does when the budget runs low.
- [The sync queue](sections/05-the-sync-queue.md) — How repository syncs are queued, retried and dead-lettered.

messages.text: How should we verify GitHub webhook signatures?

Against the raw request body, never the parsed JSON. The conventions say: "Verify a webhook signature against the raw request body, exactly as received" ([Webhooks](api-conventions/sections/02-webhooks.md)).

They also ask for delivery ids to be deduplicated in the database so a restart cannot accept a replay, and for secrets never to be logged.

citations.quote: Verify a webhook signature against the raw request body, exactly as received

messages.text: And what happens to a sync job that keeps failing?

After three failures it moves to the dead-letter queue: "A job that fails three times moves to the dead-letter queue with its last error" ([The sync queue](sync-runbook/sections/05-the-sync-queue.md)). The runbook suggests alarming on the age of the oldest dead-letter message rather than the count.

story.description:
Today the sync writes a pull request, its threads and its events in separate statements. A crash between them leaves a pull request with half its threads, and the next sync does not repair it.

### What we want
One transaction per pull request: either everything about it lands, or nothing does. The reviewer-request webhook in PLAT-301 writes through the same path, so this goes first.

body.title: Write each pull request in one transaction during sync
body.description:
Today the sync writes a pull request, its threads and its events in separate statements. A crash between them leaves a pull request with half its threads, and the next sync does not repair it.

### What we want
One transaction per pull request: either everything about it lands, or nothing does. The reviewer-request webhook in PLAT-301 writes through the same path, so this goes first.

candidates.name: Acceptance Criteria
candidates.text:
- A pull request, its review threads and its events are written in one transaction.
- A failure part-way through leaves the previous copy of that pull request untouched.
- The sync of a repository with 400 open pull requests is no slower than today.

body.acceptanceCriteria:
- A pull request, its review threads and its events are written in one transaction.
- A failure part-way through leaves the previous copy of that pull request untouched.
- The sync of a repository with 400 open pull requests is no slower than today.

findings.title: New columns have no migration
findings.body: `is_bot` and `is_bot_overridden` are added to `review_threads` in the schema, but no migration in this change creates them. The boot-time migrator will not add them, and the first write to `isBot` fails with "no such column".

findings.title: One INSERT per comment
findings.body: Still one statement per comment. Inside the transaction this also holds the SQLite write lock for the whole loop; batching per thread shortens that window.

findings.title: previousPaths is never filled in
findings.body: `deriveThreadState` reads `thread.previousPaths`, but nothing in the sync sets it, so renamed files still read as untouched. Either populate it from the files listing or add a fixture that shows it working.

findings.title: Say that derived state runs after commit
findings.body: The function comment says everything is one transaction, but `deriveThreadStates` runs after it commits. Worth one line so nobody moves it inside by accident.

findings.title: Is this filter meant to hide draft-only PRs?
findings.body: The EXISTS keeps only pull requests with a pushed commit event. Is that to hide PRs opened with no commits, or a leftover from debugging?

findings.title: Name the cron interval
findings.body:
Raised in the last review and not addressed yet. No migration in this change adds an index on `events(pr_id, kind)`.

The literal `"*/5 * * * *"` is repeated in the docs. A named constant makes the two easy to keep in step.

body.title: Refactor the upsert transaction boundaries
body.body:
Closes PLAT-292.

Writes a pull request, its review threads and its events in **one transaction**, so a crash part-way through leaves the previous copy of the PR untouched instead of half its threads.

- `upsertPullRequest` now runs inside `runTransaction` and uses `onConflictDoUpdate` instead of read-then-write.
- Thread counts for the open-PR list come from one query (`threadCountsFor`) instead of one per PR.
- Derived thread state now follows renamed files (`previousPaths`).

**Testing:** the fixture suite in `src/sync/__fixtures__/threads` passes; a 400-PR repository synced in 41s before and 38s after.

Good catch — moved it under runTransaction.

Done — extracted SYNC_INTERVAL_MS.

Consider batching these per-PR lookups into one query.
_⚠️ Potential issue_ — `botUserIds()` runs a full-table scan on every feed request. Consider caching the id set or gating it behind `excludeBots`.
_🛠️ Refactor suggestion_ — the `case when` for `is_bot` duplicates the override logic already in `setUserBot`. Extract a shared helper to avoid drift.
_🧹 Nitpick_ — `emptyCounts()` allocates a new object per PR in the loop; hoist a frozen zero-count and clone only when writing.
Micro-opt — leaving as-is for readability; the loop is bounded by open PRs.
_⚠️ Potential issue_ — a renamed file will read as `untouched` because the commit-file match is path-exact. Worth a comment noting the known false-negative.
_🛠️ Refactor suggestion_ — prefer `onConflictDoUpdate` here over the read-modify-write; it removes a round-trip and the race window.
_🧹 Nitpick_ — `is_bot_overridden` has no index but is filtered in the upsert. Negligible at this scale; flagging for completeness.
Acknowledged — not worth an index here.
**Potential issue** — `botUserIds()` scans the whole users table on every feed request. Consider caching the id set or gating it behind `excludeBots`.
🧹 Nitpick — this cast is redundant; the value is already typed as `BotId` at this point.
**Suggestion** — the `from`/`to` bounds are parsed twice; hoist the parse above the query builder.
Fair — will fold that in with the next pass.
🛠️ Refactor — this import block can be collapsed now that `sql` is unused.
Done — dropped the dead import.

ticket.title: Write each pull request in one transaction during sync
ticket.description:
Today the sync writes a pull request, its threads and its events in separate statements. A crash between them leaves a pull request with half its threads, and the next sync does not repair it.

### What we want
One transaction per pull request: either everything about it lands, or nothing does. The reviewer-request webhook in PLAT-301 writes through the same path, so this goes first.
ticket.acceptanceCriteria:
- A pull request, its review threads and its events are written in one transaction.
- A failure part-way through leaves the previous copy of that pull request untouched.
- The sync of a repository with 400 open pull requests is no slower than today.

ticket.title: Handle review-request webhooks
ticket.description:
When someone is asked to review, GitHub sends a webhook. We ignore it and wait for the next poll, so "waiting on review" is up to five minutes late.

The handler writes through the per-PR upsert, so it must land after PLAT-292.

messages.content: Is the delivery-id map a blocker on its own?

Not on its own. A replay is only accepted after a restart, and GitHub does not resend deliveries by itself. It matters more once the signature check is fixed, because then a captured delivery is the easiest way in. Keep it here if the database change is small; otherwise open a ticket and land the two blockers first.

body.title: Add CloudWatch alarms for queue depth and DLQ age
body.body:
Closes INFRA-244.

Two CloudWatch alarms on the sync queue, routed to the on-call SNS topic:
- queue depth above 500 for ten minutes
- oldest dead-letter message older than an hour

comments.body: ⚠️ Potential issue — the dead-letter alarm uses `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` on the DLQ, but `treat_missing_data` is unset, so an empty DLQ reads as INSUFFICIENT_DATA and the alarm never resets to OK.
🛠️ Refactor — both alarms repeat the SQS namespace, period and statistic; a small `locals` block would keep the two in step.
🧹 Nitpick — align the alarm-threshold constants for readability.
Will tidy in a follow-up.

body.summary: The handler does what PLAT-301 asks, but it should not merge yet: the signature is checked against re-serialised JSON rather than the raw body, and the webhook secret is written to the log.

findings.title: Verify the signature on the raw body
findings.body: GitHub signs the exact bytes it sent. `JSON.stringify(req.body)` can differ in key order and whitespace, so valid deliveries fail, and the check proves nothing about what was parsed. Use the raw body Fastify kept.

findings.title: The webhook secret is logged
findings.body: The untracked-repo log line includes `process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Anyone with log access can forge deliveries.

body.summary: The move to one transaction per pull request is the right shape. Two things hold it back: events are still written with the outer `db`, so they escape the transaction, and the comment loop issues one INSERT per comment. The rest is small.

findings.title: Events are written outside the transaction
findings.body: `upsertEvents` is called with the module-level `db`, not `tx`, so a crash after the pull request commits leaves its events missing. Pass `tx` through.

findings.title: One INSERT per comment
findings.body: Each comment is its own round trip inside the loop. A pull request with 200 comments makes 200 statements; one multi-row insert per thread would do.

findings.title: Name the cron interval
findings.body: The literal `"*/5 * * * *"` is repeated in the docs. A named constant makes the two easy to keep in step.

findings.title: Is events(pr_id, kind) indexed?
findings.body: The new EXISTS runs per pull request in the list. Is there an index on `events(pr_id, kind)`, or does this scan?

threadAssessments.excerpt: Can we batch these inserts? We do one INSERT per row inside the loop.
threadAssessments.explanation: The loop in `upsertThreads` still issues one INSERT per comment; it now runs inside the transaction, which keeps it correct but not faster.
threadAssessments.reason: Still one INSERT per comment inside the loop.

threadAssessments.excerpt: Should this run inside the same transaction as the PR upsert?
threadAssessments.explanation: Threads and events are now written with `tx` inside `runTransaction`, so they commit or roll back with the pull request.
threadAssessments.reason: Threads and events now write through the same transaction.

threadAssessments.excerpt: Is the EXISTS subquery indexed? Could be slow on large event tables.
threadAssessments.explanation: No index covers `events(pr_id, kind)`; the new EXISTS clause runs once per pull request in the list.
threadAssessments.reason: No index covers events(pr_id, kind) yet.

threadAssessments.excerpt: Consider batching these per-PR lookups into one query.
threadAssessments.explanation: `threadCountsFor` reads every listed pull request in one query.
threadAssessments.reason: threadCountsFor reads every PR in one query.

threadAssessments.excerpt: _⚠️ Potential issue_ — `botUserIds()` runs a full-table scan on every feed request. Consider caching the id set or gating it behind `excludeBots`.
threadAssessments.explanation: `getFeed` now calls `botUserIds()` once per page instead of once per item, but each call still scans the users table.
threadAssessments.reason: Called once per page now, but still a full scan.

threadAssessments.excerpt: _🛠️ Refactor suggestion_ — the `case when` for `is_bot` duplicates the override logic already in `setUserBot`. Extract a shared helper to avoid drift.
threadAssessments.explanation: The override check is repeated, but the two copies read different columns; merging them needs a schema change first.
threadAssessments.reason: Fair point, but the two checks read different columns.

threadAssessments.excerpt: _🧹 Nitpick_ — `emptyCounts()` allocates a new object per PR in the loop; hoist a frozen zero-count and clone only when writing.

threadAssessments.reason: One small object per PR is negligible here.

threadAssessments.reason: Renamed files now count through previousPaths.

threadAssessments.excerpt: _🛠️ Refactor suggestion_ — prefer `onConflictDoUpdate` here over the read-modify-write; it removes a round-trip and the race window.
threadAssessments.explanation: The read-modify-write is gone; the upsert uses `onConflictDoUpdate` on the account and node id.
threadAssessments.reason: The upsert now uses onConflictDoUpdate.

threadAssessments.excerpt: **Potential issue** — `botUserIds()` scans the whole users table on every feed request. Consider caching the id set or gating it behind `excludeBots`.
threadAssessments.explanation: Same point as the CodeRabbit thread: one scan per page now, not per item.
threadAssessments.reason: Same as CodeRabbit’s thread: once per page now.

scoring.note: While state != 'scored' no cell contains a model-derived metric at all — see absent_metrics. Every per-cell metric entry carries its own 'derivation' as well, so a model-derived figure and a code-derived figure are never renderable without knowing which is which — including after fit v2 starts emitting model metrics, when structural absence no longer protects anything.

staleness.note: corpus_age_days is AS OF generated_at and decays on disk. Recompute it against corpus.observed_at_max at read time; do not render this artifact as current.

cohortAxes.vendor: mandatory; no cell pools two vendors, at any n. A headline never compares across vendors. Catch-all vendor strings that name no product form no cell at all — see unfittable_vendors.
cohortAxes.activityBand: a RANK cut over panel_prs_per_period — MERGED pull requests in the FRAME's window (14 days for frame_2026-02-05_14d). Not a 90-day count, and not recomputed from the walk, whose per-repo merge count is capped by walk_budget. ⚠ CUT AT FIT TIME AND PER VENDOR: the panel row's own activity_band is NOT read, because it is a decile of one draw's candidate pool rather than a property of the repository, and two draws assign the same repository different bands. The number of bands is this vendor's own — see banding, and cohort.n_bands on every cell.

metricSpecs.name: acted_on_rate
metricSpecs.definition: Share of settled, fully-read vendor threads that were resolved OR followed by a human after the vendor's last comment. Deliberately EXCLUDES is_outdated — see acted_on_rate_with_outdated for the other reading; the two are emitted side by side so the sensitivity is visible rather than argued about.
metricSpecs.numerator: settled complete vendor threads: is_resolved OR human_followed_last_review_bot

metricSpecs.name: acted_on_rate_with_outdated
metricSpecs.definition: acted_on_rate widened by GitHub's is_outdated flag. A SEPARATE METRIC, never a redefinition of the one above: the two answer 'was this dealt with' under two different beliefs about whether a changed line proves it.
metricSpecs.numerator: settled complete vendor threads: resolved OR outdated OR followed

metricSpecs.name: cross_bot_overlap_rate
metricSpecs.definition: Share of this vendor's anchored settled threads whose (path, line) anchor also carries a DIFFERENT vendor's thread on the same pull request — how often two bots say something about the same line. A thread that lost its line (outdated, no line) has no anchor and is excluded from both halves rather than counted as non-overlapping.
metricSpecs.numerator: anchored vendor threads sharing (path, line) with another vendor on the same PR
metricSpecs.denominator: settled vendor threads with a (path, line) anchor

metricSpecs.name: findings_per_merged_pr
metricSpecs.definition: Non-empty comment bodies this vendor left, per merged human-authored pull request. An empty-body review (a silent approval) is NOT a finding — 89 of 1,204 bot comment rows in the smoke walk were exactly that, and counting them would score a bot that approves without words above one that writes.

metricSpecs.name: human_followed_last_bot_rate
metricSpecs.definition: Share of settled, fully-read vendor threads where a human commented strictly after the vendor's LAST comment — engagement that survived the bot's final word rather than a reply that preceded it.
metricSpecs.numerator: settled complete vendor threads with human_followed_last_review_bot

metricSpecs.name: human_reply_rate
metricSpecs.definition: Share of this vendor's settled, fully-read review threads where a human commented after the vendor's first comment. ⚠ Threads whose comment tail was truncated are EXCLUDED: 'nobody answered' and 'we did not read far enough to know' are different claims, and the corpus nulls the fact rather than defaulting it to False.
metricSpecs.numerator: settled complete vendor threads with human_replied

metricSpecs.name: median_hours_to_first_human_reply
metricSpecs.definition: Per-repository median of the time from this vendor's FIRST comment on a thread to the first human comment after it, over settled threads that got one. The clock starts at the first BOT comment rather than the thread root, because a thread a human opened and a bot joined has a root that is not a bot finding at all.
metricSpecs.denominator: settled complete vendor threads that received a human reply

metricSpecs.name: overdue_untouched_rate_168h
metricSpecs.definition: Of this vendor's review threads that were at least 168h old at observation and whose comment tail was fully read, the share that are neither resolved nor answered by a human. Threads younger than the grace window are EXCLUDED from the denominator, not counted as answered: they have not had the chance to be overdue.
metricSpecs.numerator: threads age>=168h, complete, not resolved, no human reply

metricSpecs.name: overdue_untouched_rate_72h
metricSpecs.definition: Of this vendor's review threads that were at least 72h old at observation and whose comment tail was fully read, the share that are neither resolved nor answered by a human. Threads younger than the grace window are EXCLUDED from the denominator, not counted as answered: they have not had the chance to be overdue.
metricSpecs.numerator: threads age>=72h, complete, not resolved, no human reply

metricSpecs.name: pr_comment_coverage
metricSpecs.definition: Share of merged human-authored pull requests on which this vendor said anything. ⚠ CONDITIONED ON THE VENDOR BEING LIVE IN THIS POPULATION: a repo where it emitted nothing on any merged pull request is UNDEFINED here, not 0.0 — counted under vendor_silent when there is no trace of it in the repository at all, and under vendor_absent_from_population when it reviewed only pull requests that had not merged. The floor of this metric is therefore 1/N, and that is the honest reading — 'the bot is installed but never fires' is a different claim from 'the bot is not installed', and this corpus cannot tell them apart.
metricSpecs.numerator: merged human-authored PRs with >= 1 vendor finding

metricSpecs.name: thread_outdated_rate
metricSpecs.definition: Share of this vendor's settled review threads GitHub marks outdated — the anchored lines changed after the comment. ⚠ THIS IS NOT 'likely addressed'. The host product's likely_addressed asks whether a commit touched the thread's FILE after its last comment, computed from commit file lists this walk does not fetch. The two are close enough to be confused and differ by percentage points, so they have different names and this corpus carries only the one it observed.

metricSpecs.name: thread_resolved_rate
metricSpecs.definition: Share of this vendor's settled review threads marked resolved on GitHub. isResolved is a thread-level scalar the walk observes even under comment truncation, so this metric's denominator is all settled threads rather than only complete ones.

metricSpecs.name: threads_per_merged_pr
metricSpecs.definition: Review threads carrying at least one comment from this vendor, per merged human-authored pull request. A thread two vendors both commented on counts for both — the question is what each vendor generated, not how the work was divided.
metricSpecs.numerator: review threads with this vendor in review_bot_vendors

absentMetrics.name: high_severity_share
absentMetrics.definition: Share of this vendor's findings the severity model rates major or critical. major+critical are bucketed as 'high' because CRITICAL is under-recalled and nothing auto-acts on a single label.
absentMetrics.note: STRUCTURALLY ABSENT, not empty and not zero: no cell contains this key, so a consumer cannot render a model-derived figure beside a code-derived one without knowing which it holds.

absentMetrics.name: nit_share
absentMetrics.definition: Share of this vendor's findings the severity model rates nit.
absentMetrics.note: STRUCTURALLY ABSENT, not empty and not zero: no cell contains this key, so a consumer cannot render a model-derived figure beside a code-derived one without knowing which it holds.

absentMetrics.name: distinct_category_count
absentMetrics.definition: Distinct categories this vendor emitted in a repository — the breadth half of the 'is this bot only doing one thing' question.
absentMetrics.note: STRUCTURALLY ABSENT, not empty and not zero: no cell contains this key, so a consumer cannot render a model-derived figure beside a code-derived one without knowing which it holds.

populations.outcome: human-authored, detail-observed pull requests, MERGED OR NOT. Conditioning a thread outcome on the merge selects on the dependent variable; the censoring problem merging solves for volume is solved here by settle_hours instead.
populations.volume: merged, human-authored, detail-observed pull requests. Merged because an open pull request is still accumulating comments — its count is right-censored and averaging it in understates every vendor.

unfittableVendors.reason: a catch-all for three unrelated in-house reviewers (github-actions, claude, chatgpt-codex-connector) plus every unrecognised bot fronted by github-actions[bot]. It is a cross-vendor cohort by construction, and within one repository the fold sums the products into a single unit, so even the numerator is a blend. Benchmarking a customer's in-house bot against it is the comparison rule 1 forbids.

exclusionReasons.below_min_units: live, with a non-empty population smaller than the metric's min_units. A per-repository rate over two threads is noise wearing a percentage sign.
exclusionReasons.denominator_empty: the vendor is live in this repository but this metric's population is empty — a summariser that opens no review threads has no thread-outcome rate.
exclusionReasons.repo_not_walked: the repository row is not_found or error — it was deleted, renamed or made private between the frame window and the walk. A survivorship loss, not a zero.
exclusionReasons.vendor_absent_from_population: the vendor IS live in this repository but emitted nothing inside this metric's population — typically a reviewer whose comments all sit on pull requests that had not merged when the walk read them, which leaves its per-merged-PR figures undefined while its thread-outcome figures are perfectly good. A DIFFERENT claim from vendor_silent: the bot is demonstrably installed and reviewing. Reporting either as 0.0 manufactures the 'this bot finds nothing' blind spot.
exclusionReasons.vendor_silent: the walk read no comment from this vendor on any human-authored pull request in this repository. Every rate for it is UNDEFINED — uninstalled, path-scoped and category-suppressed are indistinguishable from here, and all three are different from 'commented and was ignored'.

manifest.coverageNote: coverage figures are PER CELL and cells overlap — one repository belongs to one cell per vendor it runs. Never sum coverage across cells; use corpus.* for totals.
